newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Fighter Clark aims to be NZ's first woman PM.
newsitem.headline: Fighter Clark aims to be NZ's first woman PM.

text.p: Labour Party leader Helen Clark has survived party coups and transformed a poor television image to emerge with a fighting chance of becoming New Zealand's first woman prime minister.
Clark has timed her run to perfection as New Zealand prepares to vote in a general election on Saturday.

A group of 120 floating voters awarded her a second successive victory in the last major televised debate of the campaign on Monday, in which she reaffirmed her pledge to share the benefits of economic growth more widely.
"I cannot accept that in the middle of an economic recovery we cannot ensure that all our people have decent living standards," Clark declared.
Her metamorphosis from "ugly duckling" to "canny swan", as one commentator put it, has positioned Labour to lead a potential centre-left coalition that could end six years of conservative rule.
Clark has not been afraid to play the gender card from time to time as she has gained in confidence.
"Face up to the woman who's giving you a run for your money and who's going to take your job," she taunted Prime Minister Jim Bolger last week in a challenge to a one-on-one debate.
Clark, a 46-year-old former political science lecturer, was health minister and deputy prime minister in the last year of the 1984-1990 Labour government.
She toppled Mike Moore as leader when Labour narrowly lost the 1993 election, but came close to suffering the same fate when five leading MPs tried to oust her just three months ago.
Labour was running a poor third behind the conservative National Party government and economic nationalist New Zealand First, and only one point ahead of the left-wing Alliance.
But Clark has seized the initiative, receiving a significant boost when Moore buried the hatchet and agreed to accept a place on her frontbench team.
Her greatest success has been in the televised debates, which immeasurably lifted her morale, according to close aides.
Gone was a nervous titter and a smile that came unbidden and often inappropriately. The already deep voice was more measured.
Clark is a calm, almost passionless performer who can draw on formidable detail. She has shown a reliability and sincerity in dealing with social issues.

Some see elements of former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher about her. It is not a comparison Clark would find flattering, and she bridles at comments on her appearance when the same scrutiny is not applied to men.
Clark's message to voters is the need for better balance between economic and social policy. Spending on health, housing and education would rise. Union-hostile industrial law would go.

Whether the National Party government can push voters into backing "stability" rather than what it calls the "three-headed monster" of Labour, New Zealand First and the Alliance has emerged as the key campaign issue and will determine whether Clark's renaissance is ultimately successful.
